source.title_on_document: The Impact of Large Language Models on Open-Source Innovation: Evidence from GitHub Copilot

supplement.where: Appendices after the references in the same PDF (Appendix Tables begin PDF p. 38); the title page also links a 'Latest Version'.
supplement.holds: Table A1 summary statistics; Tables A2 and A3 triple-difference tests of the incremental-versus-substantive gap; Tables A4 to A10 robustness; Appendix B Rust/Haskell replication (Tables B1 to B18); Appendix C LLM annotation guidelines; Appendix D function-detection details.

paper_design_summary: Natural experiment at the level of open-source packages: GitHub Copilot launched in October 2021 supporting Python (and Rust) but not R (or Haskell). The authors compare quarterly commit counts of 1,187 propensity-matched Python/R package pairs (1,187 Python packages and an equal number of R packages) by difference-in-differences (TWFE, balanced TWFE, synthetic DiD), and replicate with a within-Python temporal-control design and a Rust/Haskell pair. Commits are classified as substantive (net new function definitions in the code diff; or 'Code Development' by GPT-4o from the commit message) or incremental (no new function; or 'Maintenance'). No people are assigned to conditions and no creativity rating is scored.

outcomes.name: Commits that add new functions (substantive, code-based) per package-quarter
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of commits with a positive net addition of function definitions across all files in the code diff, the substantive-contribution proxy (PDF p. 13, Section 3.3.1; p. 53, Appendix D). The analysis unit is a package-quarter pool of commits (coded set); n_units is the TWFE observation count, not a people count. TWFE standard errors are clustered by package; SynthDiD uses jackknife variance estimation. Robustness and heterogeneity variants: project activity and model upgrade (PDF pp. 24-25, Tables 6-7), logged outcome, omitted initial quarters and earlier treatment date (PDF pp. 39-40, Tables A5, A7, A9); pooled-language version in Table B16 (PDF p. 45). Availability is mixed across languages and periods; timing denotes contributions during the observation window, not a later unassisted task. No individual Copilot adoption or formal primary-outcome designation is established.

eligibility.reason: Core=no. Criterion 1 is not met: language support was a business decision, and the temporal comparison uses historical observations of the same Python packages; no people are randomly assigned AI assistance (PDF p. 15, Section 4.1; p. 18, Section 4.3; p. 26, Section 5.4.1). Criterion 2 is unclear: sample sizes count packages, commits and package-quarters; the number of analyzed people is not reported (PDF p. 12, Section 3.2 and Table 2; p. 19, Table 3; p. 41, Tables B1-B4; pp. 31-32, Section 6.3). Criterion 3 is not met under the core creativity/diversity requirement: the outcomes count actual contributions by function addition or commit-message category, rather than scoring output creativity, originality or between-person diversity (PDF pp. 12-15, Sections 3.3-3.3.2; pp. 51-53, Appendices C-D). Retained as borderline observational context because new functionality serves as an innovation/novelty-type proxy in real code output; these are raw contribution-count effects, not creativity ratings. Language-level availability does not establish individual Copilot use (PDF pp. 31-32, Section 6.3).

one_line_finding: Copilot availability raised commits to Python packages relative to matched R packages by 6.816 per package-quarter (39.55 percent; 28.40 percent in synthetic DiD; PDF p. 19, Table 3), with a smaller rise in substantive commits (new functions 0.800; Code Development 1.472) than in incremental commits (no new function 6.016; Maintenance 2.299) (PDF pp. 21-22, Tables 4-5), a gap the triple-difference terms confirm (4.979 and 0.822; PDF p. 38, Tables A2-A3).

applied.new: Natural experiment at the level of open-source packages: GitHub Copilot launched in October 2021 supporting Python (and Rust) but not R (or Haskell). The authors compare quarterly commit counts of 1,187 propensity-matched Python/R package pairs (1,187 Python packages and an equal number of R packages) by difference-in-differences (TWFE, balanced TWFE, synthetic DiD), and replicate with a within-Python temporal-control design and a Rust/Haskell pair. Commits are classified as substantive (net new function definitions in the code diff; or 'Code Development' by GPT-4o from the commit message) or incremental (no new function; or 'Maintenance'). No people are assigned to conditions and no creativity rating is scored.
applied.quote: Note: The final matched sample has 1,187 Python and R packages each.

applied.old: met | not_met | unclear; reason: Natural experiment at the programming-language level (Copilot availability for Python/Rust but not R/Haskell); no people are assigned to AI and contributors are not counted. Outcomes are counts of commits by type (new-function or 'Code Development' versus incremental or 'Maintenance'), a novelty-type proxy for exploration versus exploitation in real output, not a rated creativity or diversity measure. Borderline fit for observational context.
applied.new: not_met; reason: Core=no. Criterion 1 is not met: language support was a business decision, and the temporal comparison uses historical observations of the same Python packages; no people are randomly assigned AI assistance (PDF p. 15, Section 4.1; p. 18, Section 4.3; p. 26, Section 5.4.1). Criterion 2 is unclear: sample sizes count packages, commits and package-quarters; the number of analyzed people is not reported (PDF p. 12, Section 3.2 and Table 2; p. 19, Table 3; p. 41, Tables B1-B4; pp. 31-32, Section 6.3). Criterion 3 is not met under the core creativity/diversity requirement: the outcomes count actual contributions by function addition or commit-message category, rather than scoring output creativity, originality or between-person diversity (PDF pp. 12-15, Sections 3.3-3.3.2; pp. 51-53, Appendices C-D). Retained as borderline observational context because new functionality serves as an innovation/novelty-type proxy in real code output; these are raw contribution-count effects, not creativity ratings. Language-level availability does not establish individual Copilot use (PDF pp. 31-32, Section 6.3).
